title: Software for multi-omics data integration and analysis: a systematic and critical comparison of frameworks, packages, workflows and platforms, with EasyMultiProfiler as a featured workflow for microbiome research

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: why multi-omics integration demands dedicated software
sections.goal: Motivate the review by showing that the analytical gap is now infrastructural, not conceptual; outline the heterogeneity of tools (R packages, Python frameworks, GUI/web platforms, containerised workflows) that this review will compare; flag microbiome multi-omics as a domain with specific integration challenges that justify a workflow-level solution such as EasyMultiProfiler. Critical angle: do not equate the existence of many tools with progress — argue that fragmentation, batch effects and platform heterogeneity remain unresolved bottlenecks even as catalogues lengthen.

sections.heading: 2. A taxonomy of integration strategies: early, intermediate and late; unsupervised and supervised
sections.goal: Provide a unifying conceptual scheme that organises the dozens of tools by where integration happens in the analytical pipeline (early concatenation, intermediate joint embedding, late decision fusion) and by supervision regime. Ground each class in concrete tools — NMF/MOFA-style intermediate methods, SNF/early fusion, deep late-fusion classifiers, supervised matrix-factorisation transfer learning, and single-cell multimodal integration. Critical angle: highlight that the same tool class (e.g. graph-attention networks) is re-instantiated repeatedly for different cancers and omics with limited methodological novelty, and that early vs. late claims are often unsupported by head-to-head evaluation.

sections.heading: 3. General-purpose integration frameworks in R and Python
sections.goal: Survey reusable, method-agnostic frameworks that support customisable integration pipelines — meta-analytic packages, reproducible pipeline builders, longitudinal integrators, network-based interpreters and statistical machine-learning combinations. Critical angle: distinguish between tools that genuinely abstract integration (moiraine, miodin, timeOmics/netOmics) and tools that hard-wire a single algorithm; flag that statistical learning methods (block forest, boosting, NMF) remain competitive with deep models on tabular multi-omics despite much smaller methodological footprint.

sections.heading: 4. Microbiome-centred multi-omics tools: the case for host–microbiome integration
sections.goal: Compare tools specifically designed for microbiome multi-omics, where meta-omics layers (metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics) and host response must be aligned. Use EasyMultiProfiler as the anchor but place it alongside gNOMO (non-model organisms), CFViSA (microbiome + transcriptome) and the conceptual roadmaps from recent reviews. Critical angle: most microbiome tools still target human cohorts; cross-kingdom and non-model microbiome multi-omics are underserved; the field over-relies on 16S-derived taxonomy rather than integrated functional meta-omics.

sections.heading: 5. Web servers, GUI tools and point-and-click platforms
sections.goal: Catalogue browser-accessible platforms that lower the programming barrier — Analyst-suite components, single-cell analysts, disease-specific databases (CPMOAD, LOSTdb), radiogenomics GUIs, pathway-visualisation web servers, sandbox toolkits, and Shiny-based interfaces. Evaluate depth of analytical capability vs. ease of use. Critical angle: GUI tools often freeze specific algorithms and pre-computed cohorts, so they accelerate analyses at the cost of methodological transparency and limit customisation; database-style platforms are subject to curation drift and stale reference sets.

sections.heading: 6. Data structures, containerised workflows and reproducibility infrastructure
sections.goal: Examine the substrate on which analytical tools sit — the MultiAssayExperiment/SummarizedExperiment ecosystem, FAIR Digital Objects packaged in Nextflow, Google Cloud learning modules, and R/Bioconductor visualisation interoperability. Critical angle: the choice of container system (Nextflow, Snakemake, R packages) and metadata standard (RO-Crate, CWL, ISA-Tab) has larger long-term consequences for reuse than the choice of integration algorithm, yet receives less attention than new methods; reproducibility remains uneven across both R and Python ecosystems.

sections.heading: 7. Benchmarking evidence and evaluation criteria
sections.goal: Synthesise what existing benchmarks actually show — SNF as a strong performer for cancer subtyping, Seurat/scArches dominance in single-cell vertical integration, only modest gains from multi-omics in survival prediction, and recent head-to-head studies of biomarker discovery. Critical angle: benchmarks disagree; simulated datasets often favour different methods than real cohorts; criteria (silhouette, NMI, c-index) measure different things and the field lacks a unified panel; biomarker benchmarks reveal that many deep models fail to recover clinically actionable genes despite high accuracy.

sections.heading: 8. EasyMultiProfiler (EMP): design, strengths and limitations relative to the alternatives
sections.goal: Devote a dedicated section to EasyMultiProfiler, applying the same critical criteria used for the alternatives. Describe its five-module architecture built on SummarizedExperiment/MultiAssayExperiment, its natural-language-style pipeline, and its host–microbiome focus. Compare against general R frameworks (moiraine, miodin, timeOmics), against microbiome-specific tools (gNOMO) and against GUI platforms (MuSA, Analyst suite). Critical angle: EMP's value is the standardised five-module wrapper around an established data-class ecosystem rather than new integration mathematics; its limitations are the absence of cross-kingdom meta-omics layers and dependence on the Bioconductor release cycle; it is positioned for host-microbiome cohorts, not for single-cell or imaging integration.

sections.heading: 9. Critical perspectives, controversies and emerging frontiers
sections.goal: Discuss contested questions and forward-looking themes: trustworthy/uncertainty-aware deep models versus classical statistics; single-molecule single-cell multiomics; isoform- and TAD-level integration; network-based multilayer random-walk methods; immunometabolic spatial multiomics; AI-defined habitat radiomics; exosomal biomarker discovery; and the recurring reproducibility crisis. Critical angle: many 'emerging' tools are incremental neural architecture tweaks over a shared encoder-decoder template; reviewers should treat self-attention+GCN combinations with scepticism absent external validation; the gulf between methodological publication and clinical translation remains wide, and integration platforms often propagate batch effects unless explicitly addressed.

sections.heading: 10. Recommendations, roadmap and conclusions
sections.goal: Distil practical guidance for different user profiles (bench biologists, biostatisticians, computational method developers, clinicians) and articulate a short-term roadmap: harmonised data structures, FAIR packaging, shared benchmark panels, microbiome-specific extensions, and uncertainty-aware deep learning. Position EasyMultiProfiler as a credible workflow choice for host–microbiome research, while acknowledging the same limitations faced by any single workflow — namely, the need for complementary single-cell, spatial and clinical-grade tools. Critical angle: avoid one-size-fits-all recommendations; emphasise that tool choice should be driven by data modality, cohort size and reproducibility constraints, and that the field's most acute deficit is not new methods but standardisation.
